title: Research Explained #22 -- What Would It Take to Detect a Tiny Distortion in Spacetime?
html:
Imagine placing an extraordinarily sensitive instrument near a pair of rapidly rotating masses.

According to general relativity, rotating matter influences the geometry of spacetime. In principle, this can produce effects associated with the dragging of local inertial frames, commonly called frame dragging.

The effect is real physics. Frame dragging has been investigated experimentally in gravitational environments such as Earth's.

But what happens when we try to produce and measure an extremely small version of such an effect using laboratory-scale equipment?

That question leads us into one of the most challenging areas of experimental physics: the difference between predicting a signal and actually being able to detect it.

At Beyond the Light Barrier, we have investigated this question through a research branch identified as NP. This branch explores whether extremely small gravitational effects associated with rotating masses could be calculated and, potentially, measured using sensitive laboratory instruments.

The research progresses through numbered models and investigations. For example, NP-2C developed a numerical prediction for a particular rotating-mass and atom-interferometer configuration, while NP-2D examined whether the predicted effect could realistically be detected.

And the results have taught us something important—even though they have not produced a detectable laboratory signal.

Spacetime Is Not Completely Passive

In general relativity, gravity is described through the geometry of spacetime.

Mass and energy influence that geometry, while matter and light respond to it.

Rotation introduces additional effects. A rotating source of mass can influence the local relationship between space, time, and inertial motion.

This phenomenon is known as frame dragging.

Around a massive rotating astronomical object, the effect may be measurable with sufficiently sensitive instruments.

Around an ordinary laboratory rotor, however, the predicted relativistic influence is extraordinarily small.

That creates an interesting engineering challenge.

Could we construct a source, place a sensitive detector nearby, and distinguish the tiny relativistic contribution from everything else happening in the laboratory?

Our NP-2C Investigation

One of our research branches investigates a hypothetical laboratory-scale measurement of a weak gravitational effect produced by rotating masses.

In the NP-2C reference architecture, the modeled source consists of two effective rotating rings, each representing approximately 10 kilograms of mass and rotating at 100 revolutions per second.

The detector model uses an atom-interferometer concept involving rubidium-87 atoms.

An atom interferometer exploits the wave-like behavior of matter. Carefully controlled laser pulses can split, redirect, and recombine atomic wave packets.

The resulting interference pattern depends on differences in the phases accumulated along the modeled paths.

Under appropriate conditions, these instruments can respond to extraordinarily small accelerations and other influences on atomic motion.

Our question was whether a rotating-mass gravitational contribution could produce a distinguishable phase difference.

The NP-2C calculation used an idealized source and a specified detector trajectory. It did not constitute a complete instrument model.

Nevertheless, it allowed us to calculate a reference observable.

A Very Small Number

The frozen NP-2C effective-ring benchmark produced a predicted phase difference of approximately:

0.00000000000000011036 radians

In scientific notation:

1.1036 × 10−16 radians

A radian is a unit used to measure angles and phases.

Here, the number represents a calculated difference in the phase of an idealized matter-wave interference signal—not an angle through which a physical object visibly turns.

For comparison, one full cycle of phase corresponds to approximately 6.28 radians.

Our predicted effect is an extraordinarily small fraction of that cycle.

The calculation also produced a reference transverse displacement of approximately 8.06 × 10−27 meters within the specified model.

This displacement is an intermediate quantity in the modeled atom-interferometer calculation; it is not a proposed direct measurement with a conventional position sensor.

These numbers are mathematical and numerical predictions under the documented assumptions.

They are not measured physical displacements or experimentally observed phase shifts.

Why Predicting a Signal Is Not Enough

Suppose a thermometer could theoretically respond to a temperature change of one-millionth of a degree.

That does not mean it could reliably measure such a change in a noisy room.

The room's temperature might fluctuate. The electronics might drift. The sensor might be influenced by vibration or electromagnetic interference.

The desired signal could be completely overwhelmed.

The same problem applies to extremely small gravitational measurements.

For NP-2C, the predicted relativistic contribution would need to be distinguished from effects including ordinary Newtonian gravity, vibrations, changes in rotor alignment, laser noise, and uncertainties in the atomic trajectories.

Some of these effects can be much larger than the signal we are trying to isolate.

A correct theoretical prediction does not automatically give us an instrument capable of observing it.

What NP-2D Revealed

Our next investigation, NP-2D, examined the detector-credibility problem.

For comparison with conventional Raman atom-interferometer sensitivity, the NP-2C reference phase was translated into an acceleration-equivalent scale.

Using a reference interrogation time of 0.05 seconds, the resulting scale was approximately:

2.74 × 10−21 meters per second squared

This requires an important qualification.

The NP-2C signal is not being claimed to be an ordinary uniform acceleration. The conversion provides a comparison scale using a simplified detector response model.

It helps us ask how demanding the measurement would be.

When the predicted scale was compared with representative atom-interferometer sensitivities, the project identified an extreme statistical-sensitivity gap.

Simply repeating the measurement and averaging the results was not found to be a credible solution for the frozen historical-scale architecture.

Consequently, the NP-2D detector-sensitivity gate did not pass.

That was a negative feasibility result—not an experimental failure and not a measurement of the predicted effect.

The research had identified a potentially meaningful theoretical observable, but the specified architecture did not provide a credible path to detecting it.

Why Can't We Just Build a Better Detector?

It is tempting to assume that the answer is simply more sensitive equipment.

Sometimes improved instrumentation really does make previously inaccessible phenomena measurable.

But detector sensitivity is only part of the problem.

Imagine increasing the mass of the rotating source, spinning it faster, or moving it closer to the atoms.

Each change may increase the predicted signal under some conditions.

However, these changes also introduce engineering consequences.

Larger or faster rotors create more demanding mechanical, containment, and vibration problems.

Moving the source closer can increase ordinary gravitational influences and sensitivity to alignment errors.

Changes to the detector trajectory may affect both the desired phase and unwanted backgrounds.

These factors are coupled.

A design cannot safely multiply several optimistic improvements together while assuming that all other conditions remain unchanged.

Our subsequent NP-2E scaling work, NP-2F coupled-constraint analysis, and NP-2G material-limited screening investigated these possibilities.

The results were sobering. When realistic material-strength and rotor-speed constraints were introduced, the improvements were much smaller than some earlier optimistic estimates suggested. The simplified NP-2G screening suggested roughly 5–14-fold improvements in rotor tip speed and corresponding first-order angular momentum for representative material classes, under its stated assumptions—not the illustrative 100-fold angular-momentum improvement considered in earlier estimates.

Even those improvements did not establish a credible detection capability.

The project therefore retired the historical NP-2C rotating-source architecture as a near-term physical experiment.

This was an architecture-specific engineering decision. It did not invalidate general relativity, frame dragging, atom interferometry, or the possibility that future instruments might detect related effects.

It meant that the particular apparatus we had investigated did not justify proceeding toward construction under the available evidence and engineering constraints.

The Difference Between Noise and Systematic Error

Experimental physicists must deal with at least two broad classes of measurement uncertainty.

Statistical noise produces variations between repeated measurements.

Under suitable conditions, averaging many independent measurements can reduce its influence.

Systematic error can produce a persistent bias or a signal that resembles the effect being sought.

For example, a rotating source might generate mechanical vibrations synchronized with its rotation.

If the detector responds to those vibrations, the resulting pattern could appear correlated with the source even when the predicted relativistic contribution is far too small to measure.

Repeating the experiment thousands of times would not necessarily remove that false signal.

This is why a credible experiment needs more than a sensitive instrument.

It also needs controls, calibration, environmental monitoring, and a model of how conventional disturbances influence the measurement.

How Would We Know the Signal Was Real?

Suppose a future laboratory experiment produced a small signal that changed when the source rotated.

Would that demonstrate frame dragging?

Not by itself.

We would need to investigate whether the signal followed the predicted dependence on source rotation, geometry, and detector configuration.

We would also need to test conventional explanations.

For example, a carefully designed investigation might compare measurements with the source stationary and rotating, reverse its direction of rotation, monitor vibrations and magnetic fields, and vary the source-detector geometry.

These tests would need to be designed so that the predicted relativistic contribution could be distinguished from ordinary source-dependent disturbances.

A complete measurement model would also need to include the relevant laser, propagation, and separation phases of the atom interferometer.

Our verification roadmap explicitly identifies these requirements.

They are part of the work needed to establish detector credibility—not evidence that the measurement has already been made.

Does a Negative Result Mean We Should Stop Exploring?

It means we should stop treating the particular approach as experimentally ready.

That is different from abandoning the underlying scientific question.

The NP-2C and NP-2D investigations teach us that the historical-scale rotating-source architecture faces a severe measurement challenge.

They do not establish that every possible experiment involving weak frame-dragging effects must fail.

A different source geometry, detector technology, measurement strategy, or scientific objective could lead to a different feasibility assessment.

But each alternative must earn its own justification.

It must satisfy realistic engineering constraints, account for conventional backgrounds, and demonstrate a credible path toward a measurable observable.

The project should not proceed to hardware construction merely because the mathematical result is interesting.

What We Have Learned

Our NP research illustrates an important progression in scientific investigation.

First, we formulate a physical model.

Next, we calculate what that model predicts.

Then, we ask whether an instrument could actually distinguish the predicted effect from the environment.

If the answer is no, that finding becomes part of the scientific record.

For the frozen NP-2C reference architecture, the predicted phase was approximately 1.10 × 10−16 radians.

The subsequent detector-credibility and engineering investigations found that the measurement challenge was too severe to justify advancing that historical-scale design toward hardware.

That conclusion does not erase the calculation.

It tells us how to interpret it.

The Larger Lesson

One of the remarkable things about modern physics is that mathematics can describe effects far smaller than our instruments can presently observe.

But nature does not reveal those effects simply because we have calculated them.

We must build a bridge between prediction and measurement.

That bridge requires theoretical accuracy, numerical verification, realistic engineering, calibrated instrumentation, uncertainty analysis, and experimental controls.

Sometimes the bridge can be built.

Sometimes the calculations show that the proposed bridge is not viable.

At Beyond the Light Barrier, both outcomes matter.

Our purpose is not to produce the most exciting prediction.

It is to discover which predictions can survive the journey from mathematical possibility to physical evidence.

And sometimes the most valuable discovery is learning exactly why we cannot yet make that journey.

Sources and Further Reading

  2. Beyond the Light Barrier — Verification Roadmap v1.1. Internal research document establishing independent reproduction requirements, detector-credibility gates, uncertainty-budget requirements, and constraints on source-detector optimization.
  3. Beyond the Light Barrier — Research Method v1.2. Internal research methodology governing the distinction between theoretical predictions, numerical results, independent reproduction, and experimental evidence.
  4. Everitt, C. W. F., et al. (2011). "Gravity Probe B: Final Results of a Space Experiment to Test General Relativity." Physical Review Letters, 106, 221101. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.106.221101
  5. Bongs, K., et al. (2019). "Taking atom interferometric quantum sensors from the laboratory to real-world applications." Nature Reviews Physics, 1, 731–739. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42254-019-0117-4

Source accessibility note: The Beyond the Light Barrier project documents listed above are internal research records. They identify the documented basis for project-specific statements. Their inclusion does not imply that these records are publicly accessible or independently verified.

Research integrity note: The NP-2C phase and displacement values are numerical predictions under specified model assumptions, not experimental measurements. The NP-2D sensitivity conclusion and subsequent NP-2E through NP-2G investigations are theoretical, computational, and engineering feasibility assessments. The historical NP-2C architecture was retired as a near-term physical precursor. This article reports no new physical experiment, detection of laboratory frame dragging, independent scientific reproduction, or evidence of faster-than-light communication or propulsion.
